sound.text: The is two songs, made quickly between Japanese Cherry Blossom and Wavy Life, and SyWavy and Jett2Fly forget about it all the time. Both beats are dark and moody and hit hard without being trap, built on heavy synths and a lot of bass. It's a short phase in two songs: The Team asks for commitment, and The Oath pulls back from it.

notes.title: Krusty Krab Training Video
notes.body: The 2002 SpongeBob episode where a fish keeps yelling hoopla at the narrator until someone knocks him out with a brick. The scream is his.
He asks what it would take for the two of them to get in the zone. She likes to smoke, and smoke drifts up toward the ozone, the layer around the earth with zone in its name.

notes.title: Kumba
notes.body: The roller coaster at Busch Gardens Tampa. Its name means roar.
The opener asks for commitment in sports terms. He wants her to sign on with him as if he's filling a roster spot, and the song closes on the same ask.

notes.title: Eve
notes.body: The Philadelphia rapper Eve had a 2007 hit called Tambourine. So when he blames Eve for his rib on the next line, she's the rapper as well as the woman from Genesis.

notes.title: Adam and Eve
notes.body: In the Book of Genesis, God makes Eve from one of Adam's ribs. He blames his sore side on her, casting himself as Adam.

notes.title: Eid
notes.body: Eid al-Fitr is the feast at the end of Ramadan, the month of fasting from sunrise to sunset. Going without food leads to the end of the fast, and Eid sounds a lot like eat.

notes.title: Looney Tunes
notes.body: The Warner Bros. cartoon series, and the beeping sound is the Road Runner's. Looney here means crazy about him, and he puts his name in the middle of the title.

notes.title: SeatGeek
notes.body: The app for buying tickets to games and concerts. He's offering her the best seat in the house.

notes.title: Frozone
notes.body: The ice-making superhero voiced by Samuel L. Jackson in Pixar's The Incredibles. He shows up right after a call to stop cold, and his name kicks off a run of rhymes.
He wants a plain declaration, not a debate over her wording. Asking twice in a row shows how little room he's leaving her to dodge.

notes.title: Druski
notes.body: The Atlanta comedian known for viral skits as a shameless hustler, including his fake record label, Coulda Been Records. Moving like him means moving like a punchline.

notes.title: Wallahi
notes.body: Arabic for I swear to God, and common slang for insisting something is true. He says it two ways back to back, and coming right after a ta-da, wallah also sounds like voilà, the magician's there it is.

notes.title: Observation Haki
notes.body: In One Piece, Haki is a fighter's willpower turned into power, and Observation Haki lets the user sense what others are about to do. He's reading her the same way.

notes.title: Zumba
notes.body: The Latin dance workout that filled gyms in the 2000s.

notes.title: Uka Uka
notes.body: The evil floating mask in the Crash Bandicoot games, twin of Crash's protector Aku Aku. The game's hero is hiding in the same line.
The bridge raises the bar: being loved isn't enough, he wants to be wanted. He's sure of himself now, and whatever she's holding back can stay locked away.

notes.title: Kanye West
notes.body: Stronger and Can't Tell Me Nothing were both singles from Kanye West's 2007 album Graduation. He fits both titles into one line.

notes.title: Adele
notes.body: Adele's 2021 comeback single is a plea to be judged gently after leaving a marriage. He makes the same plea and puts her name on it.

notes.title: Khabib Nurmagomedov
notes.body: The UFC lightweight champion who retired unbeaten at 29 and 0. Kicking and beating are fight words, and a beat is also the music, so the fighter lands on both.

notes.title: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
notes.body: The Bucks and Lakers center who held the NBA scoring record for almost 39 years. A boxing jab plus the end of his name is the pun.

notes.title: Mr. Bean
notes.body: Rowan Atkinson's nearly silent British TV character, who turns simple tasks into slapstick. He's the comparison for behavior that makes no sense.
Coffee beans end up in a mug, so bean and mug belong together.

notes.title: Shundor
notes.body: Bengali for beautiful, and a name he calls himself, here in the third person. It's also on Red Lights and Life is Verses.
The verse turns three animals into accusations. The laughing scavenger stands for gossip, the fastest cat sounds like a cheater, and the king of the jungle sounds like a liar.

notes.title: Mariah Carey
notes.body: Mariah Carey's 1994 holiday hit is about wanting one person more than any gift, and the line before borrows that idea. Then her last name turns into a verb.

notes.title: 42 Dugg
notes.body: The Detroit rapper signed to Yo Gotti's and Lil Baby's labels. The words right before his name sound like his number.
Add a T to budge and you get budget, and he spells the trick out.
The oath is a vow he made to himself after getting burned: no trust, no love. The hook repeats it like he's trying to convince himself it still holds.

notes.title: Single Ladies
notes.body: Beyoncé's 2008 hit says a man who liked her should have married her. He borrows its ring for someone who wants more than he's offering.

ref.name: Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)

notes.title: The Kid LAROI
notes.body: The Australian singer whose 2021 hit with Justin Bieber is a one-word plea, the same word she keeps saying to him a few lines up. So he asks if that's who she takes him for.
The bases are the old baseball code for how far things go physically, and he casts himself as the pitcher.

notes.title: Hampton Inn
notes.body: Hilton's midrange hotel chain. He'd book a room just for her.
Here the oath cracks. He admits he's a wreck, that the girl he's with can't replace her, and that he wants her anyway, which is exactly what his vow was supposed to prevent.
